title: Joshua 5:10–12
context: Joshua 5:10–12 records the first Passover kept in the land, on the fourteenth day of the month in the plains of Jericho. The next day Israel eats the produce of Canaan, and the manna ceases. The wilderness provision gives way to the land’s harvest, a sign that the promise to the fathers is being kept. Arminian and Reformed readers share this reading of God’s faithfulness and of worship as Israel’s first act in the land.

verses.text: The children of Israel encamped in Gilgal. They kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening in the plains of Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the plains of Jericho, now that the men are circumcised as the law required (Exodus 12:48). Arminians see the people’s first act in the land as remembering God’s deliverance, with worship shaping their identity before war.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the Passover as the covenant meal that ties the conquest to the exodus: the God who redeemed them from Egypt is the God who will give them the land. Both traditions note the date follows the law’s calendar (Leviticus 23:5) and see continuity in God’s saving acts.

verses.text: They ate unleavened cakes and parched grain of the produce of the land on the next day after the Passover, in the same day.
verses.arminianNotes: The day after the Passover, Israel eats unleavened cakes and parched grain from the produce of the land. Arminians read this first taste of Canaan’s food as a concrete sign that God’s promise is now being fulfilled in their hands and at their tables.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the link with the Feast of Unleavened Bread that follows Passover. Interpreters discuss how this relates to the firstfruits law in Leviticus 23:10–14, and the text does not settle it. Both traditions see the meal as tangible evidence of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: The manna ceased on the next day, after they had eaten of the produce of the land. The children of Israel didn’t have manna any more, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.
verses.arminianNotes: The manna ceases the day after they eat the land’s produce, and from then on Israel eats the fruit of Canaan. Arminians note that God’s provision changes form, not faithfulness: the people now receive his gifts through ordinary means such as harvest and labor in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the end of the manna as a turning point in redemptive history, the wilderness provision giving way to the inheritance (Exodus 16:35). Both traditions see God providing exactly what each stage requires, whether by miracle or through ordinary harvest.
